opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more interesting strategic questions right now, and I'd push back a bit on the framing that depending on someone else's model automatically makes you fragile.

There's a real tension. If you're building a search product or a coding product on top of a frontier lab's model, you're effectively renting the core capability, and that lab can always decide to move into your market. We've seen labs ship their own coding agents and their own search experiences. So there's platform risk, and every founder in that position should be clear-eyed about it.

But the value in these products isn't just the raw model. For coding especially, what makes something actually useful is everything around the model: how you gather context from a large codebase, how you plan, how you verify changes, how you fit into a developer's workflow, how you handle long-horizon tasks without going off the rails. Those are hard engineering and research problems, and a general-purpose lab isn't necessarily going to out-execute a focused team on all of them. Distribution and product taste matter a lot too. Developers are opinionated, and if you build something they love and live in every day, that's a meaningful moat.

Where I think it gets harder is over the longer arc. As models become more agentic, more of the scaffolding you've built may get absorbed into the model. Things that today require clever orchestration might just be things the model does natively in a year. So if your whole differentiation is a prompt chain or a wrapper, that's precarious.

The companies that hold up are the ones accumulating something that compounds: proprietary data from real usage, feedback loops that let them improve on the tasks their users care about, and increasingly the ability to do their own post-training, specifically reinforcement learning on their domain. You don't need to pretrain a frontier model from scratch, but owning the RL layer for your specific problem is where a lot of the differentiated capability is going to come from. That's how you go from being a customer of the frontier to being on the frontier for your slice of the world.

So my view is: depending on another company's model is fine as a starting point, and often the right one, because it lets you move fast and find product-market fit. But you want a plan for how you become less substitutable over time, whether that's data, deep workflow integration, your own training, or ideally all three.

r001.rationale: The response notes that frontier labs can enter search or coding and create platform risk, but it does not clearly say that a successful entry could undermine startups whose advantage is a strong user experience built on those labs’ models.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify frontier providers’ ability to subsidize competing products as a disadvantage for dependent startups.

r003.rationale: The response names deep workflow integration as a way to become less substitutable and says a product developers use every day can be a meaningful moat.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most interesting questions in the space right now, and I'll admit my view on it has shifted over time.

The naive take is that these companies are in a precarious spot. They're building on top of someone else's model, the model provider can see what's working, and in principle they can just build the same product and undercut you on price because they own the underlying compute. And we've seen some of that. Every time a frontier lab ships a new capability, there's a wave of "well, that's it for the startups" commentary.

But I actually think that framing misses what the product actually is. If you look at the coding tools that have worked, the model is maybe thirty, forty percent of the experience. The rest is the harness. It's how you manage context across a large codebase, how you let the model take actions and recover from mistakes, how you handle the interface between the agent and the human, the data you accumulate about what good looks like in your specific domain. That stuff is really hard, and the labs are not necessarily well positioned to do it for every vertical. They have to generalize. A startup can go deep.

Same thing with search. The model gives you reasoning over documents, but the retrieval layer, the freshness, the ranking, the trust signals, the way you present sources, that's a product problem, not a model problem.

Where I do think there's real risk is in the middle. If what you've built is basically a thin wrapper that routes a prompt to a model and formats the output, then yes, you're going to get squeezed. The capability you're renting is going to get commoditized, and the lab or the platform is going to absorb it. The question I'd ask any of these companies is: what do you know that the model doesn't? What would be hard to replicate even if someone had the exact same model you have?

The other thing I'd say is that depending on a frontier model isn't a fixed state. The gap between the best closed models and the best open models has narrowed a lot. So the companies that are thoughtful about this are building their systems to be model-agnostic, they're fine-tuning open models for the parts of the workflow where they have proprietary data, and they're using the frontier models where raw capability actually matters. That gives you leverage in the relationship rather than being a pure dependent.

So I'd summarize it as: the ones that treat the model as a component are going to be fine, and some of them will be enormous. The ones that treat the model as the product are the ones I'd worry about.

r001.rationale: The response says a model provider could build the same product and undercut startups, acknowledging that entry could threaten them; it also explains that a strong harness can make replication difficult.

r002.rationale: It says providers can undercut startups on price because they own the underlying compute.

r003.rationale: The response describes a strong harness and domain-specific data as defenses, but does not identify deep customer integration or difficulty removing the startup as a defense.

astra-6.text:
I think the central question is: do you get better when the underlying model gets better, or does the underlying model getting better eliminate the thing you built?

If you’re a search startup, for example, you could build a really good experience around a model’s limitations today. But if the next model can do that search itself, you’re suddenly competing with your supplier. Coding has a similar dynamic. There’s a lot of value in making models useful for coding, but you have to ask how much of that value is in the model versus the surrounding product.

Depending on someone else’s model isn’t inherently a bad position. It lets you move incredibly quickly. But access to intelligence is also available to your competitors. So what compounds for you specifically? Is it the workflow you own, the relationship with the customer, or a feedback loop that helps you solve their problem better?

The strongest position is one where a better frontier model makes your product substantially more valuable, while leaving customers with a clear reason to use your product. The vulnerable position is one where your entire differentiation is something the model provider is trying to fix.

r001.rationale: It says a search startup built around current model limitations could be undermined if the model provider’s next model performs that search itself, making the startup compete with its supplier.

r002.rationale: The response notes that competitors also have access to frontier-model intelligence, but does not identify providers’ greater ability to subsidize competing products.

r003.rationale: It mentions owning a workflow and maintaining a customer relationship as possible advantages, but does not say deep customer integration makes the startup difficult to remove.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the product gets more valuable as the underlying models get better, or whether the next model release absorbs what the product does. If your advantage is getting a model to do something it’s currently bad at, that’s a pretty precarious position. You’re competing with the roadmap of the company supplying your intelligence.

But depending on somebody else’s model doesn’t automatically mean you don’t have a business. In coding, there’s a lot around the model: understanding a codebase, integrating into the developer’s workflow, running tests, and making the whole system reliable. In search, there’s the question of distribution and whether you become the place people habitually go to ask questions.

The hard part is that the frontier model companies also want those applications. So you need an advantage that compounds as models improve—something like distribution, a deeply integrated workflow, or a feedback loop that actually improves the product. Access to intelligence alone is unlikely to be the moat, because your competitors can buy that too.

r001.rationale: The response says model providers may absorb a startup’s capabilities and want the applications, but does not explain that a provider entering search or coding could undermine startups whose advantage is a strong user experience built on its models.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify providers’ greater ability to subsidize competing products as a disadvantage for startups.

r003.rationale: It names a deeply integrated workflow as a possible advantage, but does not say that deep customer integration makes the startup difficult to remove or serves as a defense against provider entry.
